questions.prompt: For a residual \(Ax - b\), the normal equations are
questions.explanation: The squared length \(\lVert Ax - b \rVert^2\) is a quadratic in \(x\). Its gradient vanishes exactly at the normal equations \(A^T A x = A^T b\). A zero residual is the special case where \(b\) is already in the column space. The same stationarity condition is valid for a tall matrix.

options: the stationarity condition of the squared residual.
a requirement that the residual is zero.
the definition of a singular value.

questions.prompt: The scalar objective \((3x - 9)^2\) is a squared residual. What value of \(x\) makes it stationary?
questions.explanation: Expanding is unnecessary. The derivative of \((3x - 9)^2\) is \(2(3x - 9) \cdot 3\), which vanishes when \(3x - 9 = 0\), so \(x = 3\). The stationary value of the objective is 0 here, and that is the objective, not the location of the minimizer.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that derives the normal equations from \(\lVert Ax - b \rVert^2\).
questions.explanation: The squared residual is a quadratic. Its gradient is \(2 A^T(Ax - b)\). Stationarity sets the gradient to zero, and rearranging produces the normal equations. The gradient formula comes before setting it to zero, and the normal equations are that condition written with the unknown on the left.
steps: Treat the squared residual as a quadratic function of \(x\).
Differentiate it to get the gradient \(2 A^T(Ax - b)\).
Set that gradient equal to zero.
Rewrite the equation as \(A^T A x = A^T b\).

questions.prompt: A one-row residual is \(a x - b\), with \(a \ne 0\). The stationary point of its square is a function of a and b. Write that \(x\).
questions.explanation: The objective \((ax - b)^2\) has derivative \(2(ax - b)a\). It vanishes at \(x = b/a\). That is the scalar normal equation \(a^2 x = a b\), divided by \(a^2\). The ratio \(a/b\) is the reciprocal of the minimizer.

questions.prompt: The column is \((3, 6)\) and the right-hand side is \((3, 3)\). The least-squares fit is one number \(x\). What is \(x\)?
questions.explanation: The normal equation is \((9 + 36) x = 9 + 18\), so \(45x = 27\) and \(x = 0.6\). The pseudoinverse of a single column \(a\) applies \(a^T / (a^T a)\) to the right-hand side. Averaging the two right-hand entries gives 3, which ignores the column.

questions.prompt: The columns of \(A\) are independent, and \(A^+ = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T\). Which statements are true?
questions.explanation: Full column rank makes \(A^T A\) invertible, and \(x = A^+ b\) is the minimizer. Then \(A^+ A = I\), so \(A^+\) is a left inverse. For a tall matrix \(A A^+\) is the projection onto the column space, not the identity on the larger space.
options: \(A A^+ = I\) whenever \(A\) has more rows than columns.
\(A^+\) is the left inverse that the normal equations build.

questions.prompt: A note writes the pseudoinverse of a tall full-column-rank matrix. Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: Independent columns give \(A^+ A = I\). They do not give \(A A^+ = I\) when \(A\) is tall. The product \(A A^+\) projects onto the column space. It is the identity on the whole output space only when the columns also span that space, which a tall matrix cannot do.
steps: The minimizer of the squared residual is \(A^+ b\).
\(A A^+ = I\) as well, because the columns are independent.
reasons: \(A A^+\) is a projection, not the identity, when \(A\) is tall.
The formula for \(A^+\) uses \(AA^T\) on a tall matrix.
\(A^+ A\) fails to be the identity when the columns are independent.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(b = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\). The pseudoinverse fit is one number. What is it?
questions.explanation: \(A^T A = 10\) and \(A^T b = 20\), so \(x = 2\). The same value is \(A^+ b\). The right-hand side is exactly twice the column, so the residual is zero and the fit is exact. Dividing the first entries, \(2/1\), happens to agree here. It is not the formula.

questions.prompt: For full column rank, which expression is the least-squares minimizer?
questions.explanation: The minimizer is \(A^+ b = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T b\). The Gram matrix that is inverted is the small one, \(A^T A\). The product \(AA^T\) is singular for a tall full-column-rank matrix. A matrix that is not square has no inverse.
options: \(A^{-1} b\), even when \(A\) is not square

questions.prompt: Three measurements of one unknown are 1, 1, and 16, and the column is a column of ones. What is the least-squares value?
questions.explanation: A column of ones makes the normal equation \(3x = 1 + 1 + 16\), so \(x = 6\). That is the average. The squared residual is a quadratic in this one unknown, and the average is its stationary point. The value 16 is one measurement, not the fit.

questions.prompt: Writing the least-squares minimizer as a pseudoinverse is the same statement as
questions.explanation: When the columns are independent, \(A^+ b\) is exactly the solution of \(A^T A x = A^T b\). A zero residual is a special case. The transpose of a tall matrix is not a minimizer, and the singular values of \(A\) are not changed by writing the pseudoinverse.
options: solving the normal equations when the columns are independent.
requiring the residual to be zero.
replacing a tall matrix by its transpose.

questions.prompt: \(A\) has rows \((1, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), and \((0, 1)\), and \(b = (1, 9, 5)\). The least-squares solution is \((x_1, x_2)\). What is \(x_1\)?
questions.explanation: The two columns are orthogonal. The first column sees the first two rows, so \(2 x_1 = 1 + 9\) and \(x_1 = 5\). The second column sees only the last row, so \(x_2 = 5\) as well. The first component is not the average of all three right-hand entries.
